96 Plus, the real debate at the Fed, more on Medicare for All, and could Congress cut tariffs?   Is this email difficult to read? View in browser                 Greg Ip   Four Ways Techruptions May Shape the Economy   Plus, the real debate at the Fed, more on Medicare for All, and could Congress cut tariffs?   The outages that took down Microsoft Outlook, air-traffic control, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase and Apple in quick succession raise a disquieting question about our hyper-networked economy.

   Could a rogue AI agent, a cyberattack, or some natural disaster shock the communications or power grid enough to be a systemic economic or financial threat?

   We are not near that yet. Reports of network problems in the week through Tuesday were the highest in at least a year, according to Ookla’s Downdetector, but the number of exceptionally widespread outages has actually been a bit below normal.

         That is no reason to ignore the economic risk, for which I suggest four templates:

   The Y2K model : Enabling computers to handle the century date change consumed vast resources before 2000. It paid off: New Year’s Day came and went without issues. Many of this week’s disruptions resulted from software patches against vulnerabilities recently identified by AI. This may be a temporary inconvenience to prevent catastrophe later.

   The 9/11 model: Unlike Y2K, many measures to prevent terrorist attacks after 9/11 weren’t temporary: more screening at airports and office buildings, no-fly lists, tougher money-laundering and customs controls. But we got used to them. Similarly, AI may never stop finding vulnerabilities, and disruptions such as this week’s may simply become background noise.

   The supply shock model: Global supply chains have been repeatedly strained or severed in recent years by pandemic, extreme weather, tariffs and war. If rogue AI agents or bad actors start to take down key systems, it would be one more source of supply shocks that undercut growth while elevating inflation.

   The Three Mile Island model : The partial meltdown at Three Mile Island in 1979 so scared the public that nuclear power development came to a virtual halt, costing society a source of affordable, zero-carbon electricity that takes far fewer lives than fossil fuels. A catastrophic AI-linked outage that slows or halts AI adoption would be similarly costly in forgone productivity.

   This is an edition of the WSJ Economics newsletter , your guide to the intersection of economics, markets and politics.   If you’re not subscribed, sign up here . 

       What I’m Following   What’s behind Fed governor Christopher Waller’s call for a 50-basis point rate increase next month? My colleague Nick Timiraos explains: “It’s less about the size of the move than about how the Fed signals. It’s a defense of the communications apparatus the Fed built over the past two decades, and a pre-emptive shot at Chairman Kevin Warsh’s potential moves to dismantle it. Two consecutive 25-basis-point increases, in December and January, would be ‘kind of the same’ as a single 50 in a normal world, Waller told CNBC on Wednesday, but only if the Fed signals the second one. Warsh has stopped giving that kind of guidance, arguing that it locks officials in and muddies the signals markets send. Waller is highlighting the trade-off: If the Fed won’t say what it is likely to do, he argues, it must act more decisively up front.”

   Medicare for All, stage one: I wrote in Tuesday’s newsletter that some moderate Democrats have ideas that don’t sound so moderate. That includes the likely next speaker, Hakeem Jeffries , who has now endorsed lowering the Medicare eligibility age from 65, while adding dental, vision and hearing coverage, and expanding coverage of children. This matches the first stage of Bernie Sanders’s Medicare for All plan. Marc Goldwein of the Committee for a Responsible Federal Budget puts the 10-year costs at: $500 billion to lower eligibility to 55; $500 billion to $1 trillion to add vision, dental and hearing; and from hundreds of billions to trillions for universal coverage for children. Healthcare expansion hasn’t always improved outcomes: A new study by Yu Liu of Tulane University and two co-authors found that older adults who gained coverage through the Affordable Care Act didn’t necessarily feel healthier or see better outcomes for conditions such as hypertension or mental health.

   Are tariffs’ days numbered? Democrats have given priority to rolling back President Trump’s tariffs. With Mary Peltola  declared the winner in Alaska , they will control 56 Senate seats come January, so they would need 11 of the 44 Republicans to override Trump’s veto. A Republican senator tells me that is possible. (Getting the requisite votes in the House would likely be tougher.) Last year seven Republican senators, four of whom are returning, and six Democrats co-sponsored a bill that would require congressional approval for tariffs to extend past 60 days. In a new report, Ed Gresser of the centrist Democratic-aligned Progressive Policy Institute would go further, requiring congressional approval “for any use of Sections 232, 301, and 201 of the trade code, or Section 113 of the recently passed Russia sanctions bill, to impose tariffs.” He advises reviewing the existing tariff schedule for anything that disproportionately burdens hourly-wage families or women, and rebuilding trade relations with allies.

       More From WSJ         • More Americans are tapping home-equity loans to pay down credit card debt, buy cars and fuel other lifestyle upgrades that would be otherwise out of reach. 

   • Chokepoints are holding back Patriot missile production . Rayon used in the missile begins as strands of fiber at a factory in the Czech Republic owned by a Thailand-based chemicals conglomerate. ArianeGroup carbonizes the fabric at its facility near Bordeaux, France, then sells the blackened rolls to Park Aerospace, which coats the material in Newton, Kan., before sending it on to L3Harris, which layers it inside solid rocket-motor nozzles for Lockheed’s Patriot factory. 

   • Early indications show strong demand for Anthropic’s shares ahead of the company’s Thursday trading debut. At $83 a share, the initial public offering values the AI model maker at around $1.5 trillion.

       What to Watch   Thursday 

   • Regional indexes from the Philly and Kansas City Feds will shed light on how economic demand has held up in the fourth quarter and whether businesses continue to face cost pressures.

   Friday 

   • 10 a.m. ET: The University of Michigan consumer survey’s end-of-month update could show whether households’ economic mood shifted after the midterm elections. The preliminary November reading, based on a survey that preceded the midterms, showed an unexpected improvement from October.

   Monday 

   • 4 p.m. ET: New York Fed President John Williams takes reporters’ questions in the Bronx, as officials wrap up their public comments before the communications blackout preceding the December Fed meeting.

       You Have Thoughts   In response to my Tuesday note about Democrats’ healthcare ambitions, Michigan reader Jim Lee writes (edited for length and clarity): 

   While both of us may have relatively little faith in the government’s administering a Medicare-for-all option well, there is one key element worth noting. Several studies demonstrate Medicare’s substantial price advantages over commercial insurers.

   Buying into Medicare at an actuarially fair price would very likely save employers a substantial sum of money. Moving Medicaid to Medicare could likely be break-even, with better access. And I’m nearly certain my Affordable Care Act insurance would be less expensive, reducing both taxpayer subsidies and individuals’ premiums.

   Thoughts on today’s newsletter? Or on the wider world? Please share them with me at wsjeconomics@wsj.com .   Include your state (or country) to be considered for publication. 

       What I’m Reading   • “Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos’s path to the ECB top job was all but assured once it became clear that he had secured what his Dutch rival [Klaas Knot] had not: a private meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace.” ( Financial Times )

   • There won’t be a food crisis, Javier Blas writes: “Food crises typically develop over the years, and the clear sign of trouble is always the same: disappearing stockpiles. This time around, thanks to the lessons of previous crises, the world entered 2026 with its granaries full.” ( Bloomberg Opinion )

       About Me   I’m The Wall Street Journal’s chief economics commentator. I’ve been writing about economics, markets and politics for more than 40 years, in the U.S. and from around the world.

Four Ways Techruptions May Shape the Economy
 
Plus, the real debate at the Fed, more on Medicare for All, and could Congress cut tariffs?
 

The outages that took down Microsoft Outlook, air-traffic control, United Airlines, JPMorgan Chase and Apple in quick succession raise a disquieting question about our hyper-networked economy.

 

Could a rogue AI agent, a cyberattack, or some natural disaster shock the communications or power grid enough to be a systemic economic or financial threat?

That is no reason to ignore the economic risk, for which I suggest four templates:

 

The Y2K model: Enabling computers to handle the century date change consumed vast resources before 2000. It paid off: New Year’s Day came and went without issues. Many of this week’s disruptions resulted from software patches against vulnerabilities recently identified by AI. This may be a temporary inconvenience to prevent catastrophe later.

 

The 9/11 model: Unlike Y2K, many measures to prevent terrorist attacks after 9/11 weren’t temporary: more screening at airports and office buildings, no-fly lists, tougher money-laundering and customs controls. But we got used to them. Similarly, AI may never stop finding vulnerabilities, and disruptions such as this week’s may simply become background noise.

 

The supply shock model: Global supply chains have been repeatedly strained or severed in recent years by pandemic, extreme weather, tariffs and war. A catastrophic AI-linked outage that slows or halts AI adoption would be similarly costly in forgone productivity.

What I’m Following

 

What’s behind Fed governor Christopher Waller’s call for a 50-basis point rate increase next month? My colleague Nick Timiraos explains: “It’s less about the size of the move than about how the Fed signals. It’s a defense of the communications apparatus the Fed built over the past two decades, and a pre-emptive shot at Chairman Kevin Warsh’s potential moves to dismantle it. Warsh has stopped giving that kind of guidance, arguing that it locks officials in and muddies the signals markets send. Waller is highlighting the trade-off: If the Fed won’t say what it is likely to do, he argues, it must act more decisively up front.”

That includes the likely next speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, who has now endorsed lowering the Medicare eligibility age from 65, while adding dental, vision and hearing coverage, and expanding coverage of children. Healthcare expansion hasn’t always improved outcomes: A new study by Yu Liu of Tulane University and two co-authors found that older adults who gained coverage through the Affordable Care Act didn’t necessarily feel healthier or see better outcomes for conditions such as hypertension or mental health.

 

Are tariffs’ days numbered? Democrats have given priority to rolling back President Trump’s tariffs. With Mary Peltola declared the winner in Alaska, they will control 56 Senate seats come January, so they would need 11 of the 44 Republicans to override Trump’s veto. A Republican senator tells me that is possible. (Getting the requisite votes in the House would likely be tougher.) Last year seven Republican senators, four of whom are returning, and six Democrats co-sponsored a bill that would require congressional approval for tariffs to extend past 60 days. • More Americans are tapping home-equity loans to pay down credit card debt, buy cars and fuel other lifestyle upgrades that would be otherwise out of reach. 

 

• Chokepoints are holding back Patriot missile production. Rayon used in the missile begins as strands of fiber at a factory in the Czech Republic owned by a Thailand-based chemicals conglomerate. ArianeGroup carbonizes the fabric at its facility near Bordeaux, France, then sells the blackened rolls to Park Aerospace, which coats the material in Newton, Kan., before sending it on to L3Harris, which layers it inside solid rocket-motor nozzles for Lockheed’s Patriot factory. 

 

• Early indications show strong demand for Anthropic’s shares ahead of the company’s Thursday trading debut. At $83 a share, the initial public offering values the AI model maker at around $1.5 trillion.

 
 
 

What to Watch

 

Thursday

 

• Regional indexes from the Philly and Kansas City Feds will shed light on how economic demand has held up in the fourth quarter and whether businesses continue to face cost pressures.

 

Friday

 

• 10 a.m. ET: The University of Michigan consumer survey’s end-of-month update could show whether households’ economic mood shifted after the midterm elections. The preliminary November reading, based on a survey that preceded the midterms, showed an unexpected improvement from October.

You Have Thoughts

 

In response to my Tuesday note about Democrats’ healthcare ambitions, Michigan reader Jim Lee writes (edited for length and clarity):

 

While both of us may have relatively little faith in the government’s administering a Medicare-for-all option well, there is one key element worth noting. Several studies demonstrate Medicare’s substantial price advantages over commercial insurers.

 

Buying into Medicare at an actuarially fair price would very likely save employers a substantial sum of money. Moving Medicaid to Medicare could likely be break-even, with better access. And I’m nearly certain my Affordable Care Act insurance would be less expensive, reducing both taxpayer subsidies and individuals’ premiums.

 

Thoughts on today’s newsletter? Or on the wider world? Please share them with me at wsjeconomics@wsj.com. Include your state (or country) to be considered for publication.

 
 
 

What I’m Reading

 

• “Spain’s Pablo Hernández de Cos’s path to the ECB top job was all but assured once it became clear that he had secured what his Dutch rival [Klaas Knot] had not: a private meeting with French President Emmanuel Macron at the Élysée Palace.” (Financial Times)

This time around, thanks to the lessons of previous crises, the world entered 2026 with its granaries full.” (Bloomberg Opinion)
